A 65-year-old man noticed
painful deviation of his right foot in
March 1996. He was admitted a few
days later because of a marked in-
crease in pain and dystonic posture
with spasms of the right leg and
lower trunk. The spasms were spon-
taneous, aggravated by stimuli, and
accompanied by autonomic hyperac-
tivity. Past medical history was sig-
nificant only for non-insulin-depen-
dent diabetes mellitus diagnosed at
50 years of age.
On neurological examination
there was equinus deformity of the
right foot, and the leg was markedly
rigid, particularly distally. V oluntary
movements of the right leg and tac-
tile stimuli often precipitated a
painful spasm that occasionally af-
fected the left leg. The rest of the
neurological examination was nor-
mal. Electromyography revealed
continuous motor unit activity at rest
in both legs and lumbar paraspinal
muscles, more prominent on the
right side. The silent period in the
tibialis anterior muscle of both legs
was normal. Results of magnetic res-
onance imaging of the brain and
spinal cord and of routine laboratory
analysis were normal. The presence
of GAD autoantibodies (GAD-Ab)
were detected by immunohistochem-
istry, radioimmunoassay (3.225 U/ml
in serum and 272 U/ml in CSF) and
confirmed by immunoblot of GAD65
recombinant protein [12]. At limiting
dilutions containing similar IgG lev-
els, the CSF dilution still showed
anti-GAD immunoreactivity when
the serum dilution was negative.
These data suggested an intrathecal
synthesis of GAD-Ab. The patient
also had pancreatic islet-cell and thy-
roglobulin antibodies. CSF examina-
tion was normal except for the pres-
ence of oligoclonal IgG bands,
which were absent in the serum. The
spasms greatly improved with di-
azepam and baclofen. One month
later the patient was readmitted be-
cause the spasms became more se-
vere and frequent, involving both
legs, and he was unable to stand be-
cause of severe stiffness of both hips
and thighs. Symptoms did not im-
prove with increased doses of di-
azepam or the addition of tizanidine
and phenytoin. Finally, treatment

with intrathecal baclofen by im-
planted pump was initiated; this led
to remission of the spasms and par-
tial improvement in the rigidity. A

course of intravenous immunoglobu-
lins (400 mg/kg per day for 5 days)
did not produce further benefit. Two
months later the patient was readmit-
ted because the painful spasms be-
came much more frequent, severe,
and accompanied by autonomic hy-
peractivity in spite of increased doses
of intrathecal baclofen. The patient
died 5 days later of septic shock.
General autopsy revealed bron-
chopneumonia. On gross inspection
the brain and the spinal cord were
normal. For microscopic examina-
tion, formalin-fixed sections from
cerebral cortex, hippocampus, basal
ganglia, medulla oblongata, cerebel-
lum, and from multiple blocks of the
cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spinal
cord were stained with hematoxylin
and eosin, luxol-fast blue, and im-
munoreacted with anti-GFAP anti-
bodies (Dakko, Denmark) and EBM-
11 antibody (Dakko, Denmark) using
a previously described avidin-biotin
immunoperoxidase technique [1].
Abnormal findings were restricted 
to the lumbar spinal cord sections.
There was a mild loss of large mo-
toneurons and many of them pre-
sented large cytoplasmic vacuoles
(Fig. 1) whereas other motoneurons
had varying degrees of chromatoly-
sis. However, spongiform changes in
the neuropil were not observed. In
addition, there was intense gliosis,
and microglial proliferation not re-
stricted to the anterior horns. These
features were also prominent in sec-
tions with no vacuolar changes and
extended to the thoracic spinal cord
sections.
This case illustrates that the clini-
cal picture of SMS is not uniform.
The acute onset, the initial restriction
to only one leg, and a relentless and
progressive course that led to the
death of the patient only 8 months
after the onset of the symptoms is
relatively uncommon in SMS. The
rapid course of this patient was more
suggestive of progressive encepha-
lomyelitis with rigidity a disorder
characterized by rigidity, signs of
brainstem involvement, and neuronal
loss with inflammatory infiltrates in
the nervous system at autopsy [3, 4].
Although our patient had some atypi-
cal features according to established
SMS criteria [5], we consider SMS
as the most likely diagnosis based on
the following considerations: (a) typ-
ical clinical features once the full-
blown clinical picture was estab-
lished, and the absence of neurologi-
cal signs other than those related to
SMS without CSF pleocytosis; (b) a
characteristic EMG, with a normal
silent period; (c) positive oligoclonal
IgG bands, and (d) the presence of
GAD-Ab in serum and CSF, associ-
ated with clinical and serological ev-
idence of organ-specific autoimmu-
nity. Although GAD autoimmunity is
not restricted to SMS [12], GAD-Ab
are a useful marker of SMS in the
setting of appropriate clinical and
electrophysiological features [13].
Pathological examinations of the
central nervous system in patients
with SMS have not shown consistent
changes, suggesting that SMS dys-
function is due to a functional rather
than a structural disturbance [6, 10,
16]. The most frequently reported
changes have been variable, usually
mild, neuronal loss in the anterior
horns and gliosis (Table 1). Perivas-
cular lymphocyte cuffing has been
described in two SMS patients [8, 9],
one of them associated with GAD-
Ab [9]; however, the severity of the
infiltrates was mild compared to that
observed in autopsy studies of pro-
gressive encephalomyelitis with ri-
gidity. In spite of the absence of in-
flammatory infiltrates, the presence
of oligoclonal IgG bands in the CSF

of our patient suggests that lympho-
cyte invasion of the nervous system
occurred sometime during the evolu-
tion of the disease. An explanation
for the absence of infiltrates in the
autopsy findings could be the previ-
ous treatment with high-dose intra-
venous immunoglobulins. However,
the progression of the symptoms dur-
ing this treatment would suggest the
persistence of the infiltrates.
The most prominent finding in the
present case was the presence of vac-
uolar degeneration in the cytoplasm
of many anterior horn cells in the
lumbar spinal cord. The correlation
with the clinical symptoms suggests
that these pathological features are
relevant. Isolated vacuolar changes

in the cytoplasm of motoneurons is
an unusual pathological feature. Mi-
crovacuolar degeneration of the mo-
toneurons may be seen in mice car-
rying a transgene for mutant human
Cu,Zn, superoxide dismutase, a gene
whose mutation has been linked to
familial amyothophic lateral sclerosis
[2]. A vacuolar degeneration similar
to that of our patient has been de-
scribed in a patient with spinal my-
oclonus [14]. In both studies, as well
as in the present case, vacuolization
appeared only in the body of large
neurons of the anterior horn but not
in the neuropil or others cells, sug-
gesting a selective involvement of
the motoneurons. It has been sug-
gested that the vacuolar changes cor-
respond to an increased excitability
of the motoneurons [2, 14]. This hy-
pothesis would fit well with the pre-
sumed pathogenesis of SMS that
postulates an imbalance between ex-
citatory (catecholaminergic), and in-
hibitory (GABAergic) pathways con-
trolling a -motoneuron activity [7].
Unfortunately, detailed studies of the
GABAergic neurons in the spinal
cord of SMS patients are scarcey.
Warich-Kirches et al. [17] found a
reduced size of inhibitory interneu-
rons in the spinal cord of a SMS pa-
tient. Similarly, a selective loss of
small and medium-sized neurons of
the anterior horns of the spinal cord
has been found in the autopsy of a
patient with progressive encephalo-
myelitis with rigidity [3]. Future 
autopsy studies should try to obtain
nervous tissue in optimal conditions
to study the GABA-ergic neurons of
the spinal cord.
